Karsten Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo
Yeah. We do have a good sense of that because that's the core of the entire decision case to access additional capacity. Do bear in mind that we are already working with Catalent as a CMO. There are lines working for Novo Nordisk already with Catalent. What we're getting is additional capacity on the different lines at the different sites. Of course, we honor the contracts that are in place with the existing customers. They have to run off. Let's say the deal closes by end of this year, then we'll have to do technology transfer to the new lines also during 2025.
You could say additional capacity beyond what we have already contracted as a CMO will gradually start from 26 and onwards.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Karsten. We'll go to Emily. Oh, sorry. Yeah, over here, same table.
Kritika Talia
Analyst, Berenberg
Hi, Kritika Talia from Berenberg. Just a question on Wegovy access. We've heard that certain employers have reversed their initial decisions to provide access to obesity medications just because of the escalating demand and associated costs. Is this a trend that you have seen? Related to that, could you just provide us an update as to your current formulary access and specifically the proportion of covered lives that have employer opt-in? Thank you.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
In terms of the employer opt-ins, Camilla, would you give that a go?
Camilla Sylvest
EVP and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo
First of all, we have, you know, more than 50 million patients being covered in the US, so very strong access. Around 80% of them pay up to only $25 per script in terms of self-pay. When it comes to opt-ins, there will always be opt-ins and opt-outs, but we continue to have a net opt-in, so to say, of employers. It just means that we continue to broaden our access.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Camilla. The last question will go to Emily before we round off.
Emily Field
Director and Head of US Biopharmaceuticals Equity Research, Barclays
Hi. Emily Field from Barclays. A somewhat similar question, but going back to the question of stay time, you know, how much do you think that insurance coverage in the US deflates or dampens stay time just with people switching jobs, aging into Medicare, and so they might not have coverage to that degree? I mean, do you see that as also a big dampening effect in addition to supply constraints?
Camilla Sylvest
EVP and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo
Yeah. I think, you know, there will always be people that may opt from one team to another where they are not covered or so, and that of course happens. Given that 50 million lives are covered, I think we don't need to be preoccupied with the potential in terms of coverage. Also keeping in mind on stay time, it's really in the first sort of 60 days that we really see the drop-offs, probably part of getting used to GLP-1. Then once people continue to stay on, they stay on longer. Keep in mind that if six months is truly an average, and you have to think about the variation in this.
Of course, that's also why there's significantly higher stay time for people who have been on GLP-1 before, most likely because they are either used to, you know, you know, being initiated on GLP-1, knowing more what to expect, and therefore, the average stay time is much longer. Think about it much more like that. We think, you know, we're treating one million patients now, but 50 million being covered, this is not what is, you know, what is holding anyone back. To the point from before, we're truly scaling production, you know, to be able to supply more doses into starter doses so that people can start and continue on the treatment. That's really what we are working on right now.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Camilla. Before handing it over to you, Lars, for final remarks, thanks to everybody in the room for coming and for everyone online for dialing in. In case of any follow-ups, please reach out to Investor Relations. Lars, final remarks.
Lars Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo
Thank you. I hope it comes across that we are very pleased about where we are as a company, both in terms of our traction with, say, sema and other products, not least in the US market. We upgrade because we have more supply coming, and we upgrade in value, so don't need to worry about, you know, the price per script, so to say. A lot of questions. I appreciate that on pipeline because we have a really exciting H2 of the year, not only in growth point of view, but also in terms of inflection points for pipeline, and I think Martin had some good points there. Thank you very much for your interest.
We look forward to share more details on all these aspects, as they evolve over time. Thank you.

content.text:
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to the revamped Sterling Square at Citibank. Good afternoon to everyone in the room and to those listening in on the webcast. Good morning, good afternoon, good evening. It's been a very busy week for earnings and other events. We are ending the week on a high with the Q1 London Roadshow of Novo Nordisk. The speakers don't really need introduction, but just notice Karsten, Group CFO, Camila, Group Commercial Strategy Head, and last but not least, Martin, Head of R&D, joined by an array of investor relations. Now, usually I'd be saying without further ado, hand straight over to Karsten for some slides and some Q&A.
[Company Representative] (Citi)
Company Representative, Citi
I think it is worth us just pausing and recognizing that it is Daniel Muusmann Bohsen, his last function as the head of Novo investor relations. I think that needs to be sort of recognized by the audience in the room. Not just yet, not just yet. Got a few more words to say. On that note, I have known Danny, I think, for over 15 years. He was a Willis Towers Watson, Novo junior IR, and I was still a Willis Towers Watson analyst covering Novo Nordisk, and we were discussing Insulin and Victoza back in the days. I think with Martin's blessing, he was sent off to Colombia to go and sell some drugs. Then came back in 2020 to be a head of investor relations.
I think we can all agree, being head of IR in 2020 to 2024 for Novo, not a bad place to be. Daniel, I mean this, and hopefully I'm speaking on behalf of everyone here and on the line, you know, your professionalism, your patience dealing with people like ourselves, your responsiveness, helpfulness, and just all around being a good bloke, really appreciated. We wish you well on your next venture with Novo Nordisk. Plenty of good times I'll have to say. Just call out, I think New Orleans 2016 was a particular highlight. Thank you for making that one special. Just before we say goodbye, Daniel, and wish him well, I do have a little gift for you.
It's within my compliance policy of less than $25. It is to help you immerse yourself in the Taiwanese culture. Daniel, on behalf of everyone here, I do wanna say thanks for everything and good luck going forward. Thank you. I will be asking Karsten about Taiwan and the sort of change in performance over the next few quarters under new management. Thank you.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Great. Thank you, Pete, for those nice words to Daniel. We are all sad he's leaving, but we're also very much looking forward to follow him in Taiwan. You know, we have a materiality assessment on what we report externally in terms of our segment split and so on. Every week we'll be tracking in our weekly sales if Taiwan sales is becoming big enough to include in the quarterly external announcement. We're all rooting for you, Daniel, for Taiwan to make one of the coming quarters. Thank you to Pete and Citi for hosting in your beautiful new premises here. Nicely revamped, so we appreciate that.
then we're bringing another strong quarter from Team Novo in terms of performance. continued growth, continued momentum from last year, amongst the strongest growth stories in the industry, as you know, and we keep pushing that. as you know, the future's uncertain, and it might play out differently. hence we have a nice deck with a forward-looking statement included, so no further details on that. every quarter, we bring a status on our strategy execution, and I'm not gonna go through all the details. you'll hear a lot more about it in the coming hour. just to say on the environmental side, we keep pushing forward.
Now we started reporting on full Scope one, two, and three. You see that being up 32%. There's one singular key driver for our CO2 emissions being up that much. That is the fact that we're building a lot of new factories, which goes directly into our scope three emissions. We don't take it lightly, but now we're fully transparent around our environmental footprint. 42 million people now on Novo products, up 4 million compared to a year ago. Continued strong commercial execution that Camila will come back to. I think actually one of the biggest years ever in Novo history in terms of the magnitude and importance of R&D readout.
I'm getting an echo from the new audio. I'll keep talking. The net 24% sales growth. Really pushing on all fronts. You'll hear much more. Without further ado, over to Camila on commercial execution.
Camila Sylvest
EVP of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Karsten. Just to recap on our sales growth numbers, this Q1, we had 24% sales growth, 30% operating profit growth. As you can see from the slide here, 35% growth in North America and 11% growth in international operations. The growth is really driven by GLP-1. We see a 32% growth in GLP-1 in diabetes, 42% growth in obesity. We are very pleased with the progression of course our GLP-1 business, both in diabetes and in obesity. On total diabetes, we continue to gain market share. We have also increased market share this last quarter and now at 33%.
If we now look at the obesity business here, you see a gradual increase of supply continue to expand our obesity business. We very much of course understand that at this point in time, the obesity business is a lot driven by the supply into the market. The underlying business is performing very well. There are no major changes to that compared to last year, so we continue to be happy with the progression that we see here. We have gradually increased our supply of the lower dose strength since May last year. Again, from January this year.
The broad commercial access on the formularies means that we have approximately 50 million lives covered in the U.S., and we have now also launched Wegovy in nine countries in International Operations plus Canada, so that means 10 countries now where we have made Wegovy available. We'll probably talk a little bit more about that later. Now I'll just hand over to Martin to say a few words about R&D.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you very much, Camila. As you all know, we conducted a small study called SELECT that read out last year, and we were very excited about the results. We're actually equally excited about the update to the U.S. label that we've received during this quarter. Obviously, we get the CV indication indicating that semaglutide is associated with a 20% risk reduction from MACE, major adverse cardiovascular event. That's myocardial infarction, a stroke, and it's cardiovascular death. On top of that, this risk reduction is now reflected in the label, achieved regardless of baseline gender, age, race, ethnicity, body mass index, and baseline renal function.
On top of it, we also saw we were allowed to indicate the data despite the fact that that it was outside of the testing hierarchy, where we see a 15% numerical reduction in cardiovascular death and a 19% significant reduction on all-cause mortality. That is now reflected in the label, which obviously is something that we are very, very excited about. In addition, the FDA has indicated that the mechanism of the CV benefit is not fully understood, indicating that that benefit is associated with more than just the body weight loss. This is something that we've talked about a couple of times. We see something in semaglutide that goes above and beyond body weight loss when it comes to the CV benefit, potentially also the renal benefits that we have observed with the molecule.
In line with our broader cardiovascular strategy, we are continuing to do acquisitions to both our pipeline. As you know, our focus when we talk about cardiovascular disease is not any cardiovascular disease. It's basically in the broader metabolic aspects of cardiovascular disease. Key focus is on ASCVD and inflammation, and on heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. We recently acquired a company called Cardior having a lead assets which was an A or is an ASO targeting microRNA-132, which is directly involved in heart failure pathophysiology. This goes directly into our strategy of expanding our cardiovascular presence. We're focused on heart failure. We're focused on the ASCVD, and we're very excited about progressing the cardio assets into further clinical development. These were just two highlights.
Obviously, it's quite exciting, as Karsten also alluded to be in R&D Novo Nordisk these days. We do see progress across all of our therapy areas. Obviously, we keep focus on diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obesity, and rare blood disorders, but we do also see progress in our hepatology focus, specifically semaglutide for NASH, where we will see the readout of the ESSENCE phase III trial later this year. We also see progress in our renal, obviously exemplified by FLOW. That basically means that we continue to press on all cylinders and see very successful readout, very successful initiations, throughout the course of the year. This, I think, is almost gonna be the quiet quarter because moving into the later stages of this year, we are looking towards two advisory committees with the U.S. FDA.
One is on insulin icodec. Insulin icodec has already received a positive CHMP opinion from the European authorities. It's approved in Canada and Switzerland, and it has an action date in U.S. in July. The outcome for insulin icodec in U.S. is focused specifically on type one diabetes. The outcome is also from a timing perspective placed so that this is in due time for the action date. It's gonna be a good discussion. We have been informed that the committee will not discuss the type two indication, which we've already discussed is clearly demonstrating a very nice benefit risk, but also some very nice convenient benefits of insulin icodec in this space. The other advisory committee hearing is gonna be about heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and semaglutide. This is a huge upside.
As you know, we conducted the STEP-HFpEF trials with the purpose of looking at six-minute walk test and Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire. In those two studies we also saw hard endpoints, heart failure, hospitalization, and cardiovascular death. When we submitted the data, the FDA actually granted us both priority review, indicating that the data are actually exciting, clinically relevant, but also coming from two small studies. We also got the advisory committee hearing to discuss the impact of it. Again, a huge upside for semaglutide specifically with Wegovy. I can feel Karsten is becoming impatient, so I have to start focusing.
Maybe just calling out that in a couple of weeks we'll see the long-awaited data in our franchise from EMA, which obviously also could potentially be something very exciting. With that, back to you, Karsten.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Martin, for an elaborate walk through of the slides. As always. Joking aside, amazing year from R&D in terms of readouts and actions. I cannot remember a year where we've had so much action and so many readouts and decision points, so really important to deliver on this. Q1 results, you've all seen it in our company announcement. Coming back to a 24% growth, continuing the momentum from last year, the same growth drivers being Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus. In the quarter, we had a one-off in terms of an accounting estimate adjustment which pumped up growth by 5%. Adjust for that, we're in the 19% range.
Yes, last year's comparator was easier, but then there are some supply issues. Just to say the run rate in Q1 is around 20%, apples to apples. In terms of our capital and resource allocation, as I covered at the Capital Markets Day, of course we continue to drive productivity but a broadly stable gross margin. Lower growth in commercial investments than sales growth, simply due to the fact that we have the infrastructure in place and the demand nature of our products. On the other hand, linked to the slide here you just saw, a lot of opportunities in R&D, so really pushing to expand and broaden our R&D pipeline, stepping up R&D investments by 28%.
All in all, operating profit up 30% and our earnings per share up 29% for the quarter. Outlook for the year. If you adjust for the accounting estimate adjustment in Q1, then our guidance is unchanged at constant exchange rates, but bumped by 1% linked to the one-off. Now our full year expectations are between 19% and 27% on top line growth and 22% and 30% on OP. Then given the strengthening dollar, currencies are a little bit more favorable, which are then in turn offset by our hedging losses on the net financials. All right, this covers the formal presentations, and then we have Daniel Bohsen facilitating his last Q&A.
We look forward to that and of course any specific questions on Taiwan. Daniel is more than open to cover them himself. Should we move to this?
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Yeah, no, Camila has been General Manager for region China, so she will cover those questions today. Please state your name and institution. Let's go with one question per person, then we can take several rounds. Emily had her hand up very fast.
Emily Field
Director and Lead Analyst European Pharmaceuticals, Barclays
Hi. Thank you. Emily Field from Barclays. I'm not gonna ask directly about the competitor data overnight, but when could we expect to see the phase I data from your once-monthly GLP-1 GIP? You know, how important do you think it is to have dose and convenience that goes beyond once weekly?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Martin, I think this one is for you. A few words on that, our progress there.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo Nordisk A/S
The study for the once-monthly GLP-1 GIP is gonna be ongoing. We expect to see the readout around the turn of this year. In terms of the importance, I think the current dynamics as I see it, and obviously Camila can also speak to that. There's a clear driven by efficacy over preference or anything else in this space. Our question when we have stuff in our pipeline is always, is it differentiated efficacy? Then obviously the convenience becomes a secondary factor. We will continue to pursue that, but efficacy as I see it comes first.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Let's go to Simon.
Simon Baker
Partner and Head of Global Biopharma Research, Redburn Atlantic
Thank you. Simon Baker from Redburn Atlantic. I too will refrain from asking you to comment on someone else's data that nobody's seen. Just in terms of how you see the market evolving over time, it seems highly unlikely that it'll be the same in 2030 as it is today, because of your own products that you have as well as others. It also seems unlikely that everything else outside Novo that's in development will fail. Equally unlikely everything will work. What's your assumption of how this market will evolve both through your own portfolio evolution and the efforts of others? Thank you.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Camila, I think, can you give some perspectives on the obesity market, how we think it will develop?
Camila Sylvest
EVP of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk A/S
Yes, Simon. If we take a starting point in the number of people living with obesity, we know that there are more than 800 million. We know of today, we are helping treat, you know, less than a million in terms of fully equivalent patients, if we may call it like that. That basically means that there's ample opportunity to grow in this space and to help many more patients. It's likely that there will be, you know, different segments in the future where the higher efficacy segment is, of course, where we have our strong focus. From a science point of view, we have a strong label now with the SELECT on Wegovy, where we are addressing not just weight loss, but also beyond weight loss cardiovascular risk profile. We know that is what people die from.
31% of everyone dies from cardiovascular issues. Now, we have also, of course, our FLOW data. To complement, you know, Wegovy's label with that is, of course, a lifecycle management plan for us. In addition to that, we are then bringing on new compounds with also, hopefully, greater efficacy. It's not to say that there will not also be a space for a high convenience product, maybe with lower efficacy. Having said that, today there are two companies that are competing in this space. It's still early days. There's probably room for more, just given the magnitude of the numbers. I do expect that we've seen a lot of progress in the last few years on physicians that are willing to prescribe obesity products. Just a few years back, we all remember it wasn't exactly like that.
There has been a lot of development, and hopefully it will mean we can address more of these comorbidities related to obesity. That, of course, clearly goes beyond just weight loss.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thanks, Camila. Let's move over here. Yeah.
Evan Seigerman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, BMO Capital Markets
Hi, there. Evan Seigerman from BMO Capital Markets. I'm not gonna ask about the FTC second request because I know that's not you specifically. I did wanna ask about how much more capacity do you think you can get from the three facilities from Catalent, and what does that do to the supply of all of your products, you know, by 2026? Thank you.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Evan. Karsten?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Yeah. In terms of FTC, to cover that one first, it's completely normal that when you have a big transaction that there's a process with the FTC to assess any antitrust considerations. There's nothing unusual there, and we have no changes in our expectations and in terms of deal certainty and confidence in that, just to cover that piece. As to scalability, we're no doubt explicitly guiding on the magnitude. If you look at our current footprint on fill finish, you know, where we have around a handful or so of filling sites today, then adding three filling sites of varying sizes, this is a meaningful step up in capacity on our overall fill finish.
I would say on the single-dose syringes, we have very limited capacity in-house today, so that's mainly a CMO setup. With this change, then we take a key platform for the company. We use it for currently Wegovy U.S. as a main product, but then we take a very important production platform in-house under full control. So there's also a risk control element to what we're doing here, but a significant step up. The important part, the reason why we do it, just to remind you, this is about speed and scale. It is to step up capacity as fast as possible compared to other alternatives.
Evan Seigerman
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, BMO Capital Markets
Thank you.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Karsten. Thanks for the question. Jo?
Jo Walton
Pharma Analyst, UBS
Jo Walton, UBS. It's along the same lines in terms of capacity, so I guess it's for Camila, this one, though, perhaps. In the market today for obesity, people have moved from Saxenda to Wegovy. They've really moved up and not stayed at the lower efficacy. So let's just assume that CagriSema has good data. Should we be assuming that you would expect pretty much everyone to move from Sema to CagriSema? 'Cause that seems to be an even more difficult manufacturing problem, given that cagrilintide you're making externally. I just wonder whether governments, particularly when Sema is cheaper, if it's in IRA, will say, "That's good enough," and that Sema will be your base load of product, and then CagriSema will just be reserved for the, you know, more difficult patients.
That it's more, perhaps, Simon's question about how the situation evolves and whether we should think of that transition that we've already seen moving to the next one or not. Thank you.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Jo. Camila?
Camila Sylvest
EVP of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thanks, Jo. I think you are right. It's a completely different situation than what we have with Saxenda and Wegovy, not least just for the very efficacy of what we have on Wegovy today, including the SELECT trial that Martin has just presented. Because of the magnitude of the numbers and because of the number of people being treated, plus the need and the demand out there, it's more likely to see an expansion of the market with new products coming in and a very strong base, of course, with Wegovy also into many years into the future. I would not see this whole, you know, additional of a strong pipeline as purely a cannibalization exercise.
It wouldn't be the right thing to do because we have so many patients that needs to be treated, and some need a higher, you know, focus on weight loss, others need higher focus on comorbidities. There is a position for also new innovations that are add-ons to the existing base that we are developing for many years into the future with Wegovy also.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Camila. Let's go to James.
James Quigley
Executive Director, European Pharma and Biotech Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Thank you. It's James Quigley from Goldman Sachs. I've got a question for Martin on muscle sparing. So what are you hearing from doctors in terms of if there's like a desirable ratio in terms of fat loss versus muscle loss in terms of or is it more of a case of just losing the weight in general? And then as you think about SELECT versus STEP 1 and SUSTAIN 8, where it's 40% lost from lean body mass. Have you seen any data from SELECT that suggests that flips over time or gets a bit better? Thanks.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo Nordisk A/S
What we hear from treating physicians is that that is currently not a consideration. I think it comes from a lot of these physicians have introduced weight loss with non-drug interventions for a period of time. If you look into sort of the broader literature, when you introduce a weight loss, the proportional weight loss coming from lean body mass is typically somewhere between 25% and 45%. The driver of that ratio between lean body mass loss and fat mass loss is typically the speed of weight loss. When you have a proportional weight loss from lean body mass around 35% to 40%, that's actually within that realm.
That basically means that that is a normal and healthy weight loss. You could actually argue, and this is obviously also why we are super happy with data from SELECT, we can actually show even in cardiovascularly sick patients, so presumably slightly more frail patients, we show that we improve not only cardiovascular morbidity, but actually also all-cause mortality. That basically, again, just plays into this appears to be a healthy weight loss. Based on current treatment, I don't see this as a bigger problem. I think it has to be a focus area, also with current treatments, in particular in frail patients. When we move into the potential for bigger weight loss, it has to continue to be a focus area.
This is where we take some comfort from the Amylin biology because based on animal studies, both from us but also from others, Amylin appears to be associated with an even bigger improvement of the lean to fat mass ratio. We didn't do body composition assessment in SELECT, so I don't have any data from there. Again, based on what we see, also based on the actual outcomes for patients, do they live longer? Do they live healthier? We are quite comfortable with what we see right now.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Martin. Thank you, James. Let's go to Sachin here on the first row.
Sachin Jain
Assistant VP, Bank of America
Sachin Jain, Bank of America. Perhaps for Karsten, on S&D phasing through the year alongside supply. The question is, Q1 S&D and the full year guide obviously implies inflection spend through the year. Any color on what is gating that inflection in spend? Is it linked to an inflection in supply? And is the supply inflection linked to whatever promotional activity you do around Ozempic or Wegovy? For example, SELECT or heart failure towards year end? Thank you.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Sachin. Karsten, any comments on S&D phasing?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
S&D in the quarter was 20% of sales. Full year, we're looking at more around 22% or so, something like that in terms of S&D ratio. You are correct that our S&D phasing is slightly backloaded. Of course that's linked to our commercial strategies, and our commercial strategies are linked to supply availabilities as well as R&D readouts. For instance, now we've had SELECT and now we'll start promoting even more based on the updated label from SELECT. That of course entails some promotional spending linked to that in the U.S. as a specific example. You shouldn't link it directly as a direct causality that then there's more out of manufacturing in a specific quarter.
Of course it's all tied together in a logic. I think that's as precise as I can give it.
Sachin Jain
Assistant VP, Bank of America
On R&D, sorry, is there anything other than SELECT that you'd call out?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
In terms of readouts?
Sachin Jain
Assistant VP, Bank of America
Yes. You said commercial linked to R&D other than SELECT. Is there anything? Sorry, apologies.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Yeah.
Sachin Jain
Assistant VP, Bank of America
You said commercial linked to R&D.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Yeah.
Sachin Jain
Assistant VP, Bank of America
Other than SELECT. Is there anything else that we should be thinking about this being linked to?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Well, you could say, in terms of weekly launches, there'll of course be some launch preparations taking place there. Then, Martin's infamous pipeline slide there, you saw that, you know, if whatever we get in terms of feedback from the advisory committees also on HFpEF, will impact our commercial strategies for the rest of the year.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Sachin. Thank you, Karsten. We can go to Richard.
Richard Parkes
Pharmaceuticals and Biotechnology Equity Analyst, BNP Paribas Exane
Yeah. Richard Parkes from BNP Paribas Exane. It's a follow-on from a question I asked yesterday, but it's on the same theme related to potential segmentation of the market, 'cause obviously the other companies are making a bet that if you can develop a scalable oral, then you can unlock a much broader opportunity and maybe less severely obese people with overweight and health issues. So you've placed your bet on monlunabant, which I suppose my question is, how confident are you that the drug isn't getting into the brain and therefore won't have the psychiatric side effects? Because we see other companies, they're developing CB1 inhibitors, arguing about who's got the best data on drug's ability to penetrate the brain.
What underpins your confidence that the drug isn't getting into the brain and therefore unlikely to cause those side effects?
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Martin, this one's for you.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo Nordisk A/S
Yeah. Thank you. We are quite confident that the brain penetration is substantially less than what has been the case for previous drugs in this class. We never talk about ruling out some brain penetration. If you look back at the historical cases, it was actually about exposure, and therefore, with the very low penetration that we expect to potentially see here, based on the data, also clinical data that we've seen so far, we are not concerned. We take it seriously, and that's also why you will actually see us. Normally I'll talk about the speed to going into phase III and further development. In this specific case, we actually specifically wanna do a large scale phase II study with the purpose of ruling out any new psychiatric risks.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Martin. We can go to, Laura. Hope there's a mic to guide you.
Laura Hildey
Equity Research Analyst, Berenberg
Thanks. Laura Hildey, Berenberg. Just going back to the once-monthly. What is the latest on applying your once-monthly technology to your other pipeline assets? So could you apply it to amycretin, CagriSema? And if not, what's the limiting factor? And does once-monthly tie into why you've progressed the GLP-1 GIP combination, even though it's a once-weekly progression? Thanks.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you. Martin, that's also for you.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo Nordisk A/S
We have actually several different modalities for protected action. Obviously the one that we have in the clinic right now is attracting some attention that could potentially be applied elsewhere. We currently have, as I said, several modalities being investigated in the preclinical space. What we, at the end of the day, will move forward also into later stages development depends obviously on the efficacy, but also the potential for scalability. We're not committed to anything yet, and you have to see the current ongoing once-monthly with GLP-1/GIP as an exposure study to investigate the technology.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you. We can go to Peter.
Peter Welford
Research Analyst, Jefferies
Hi, Peter Welford with Jefferies. Can I come back to the topic that we came up a while ago on Wegovy in terms of the different sort of formulations or types that could be available in the U.S. and sort of in general, the U.S. strategy. Have you revised at all your thinking in terms of sticking with a single-use pen in the U.S. market and not, you know, launching any other alternatives? Equally, any thoughts on a sort of direct distribution system that I think one of your competitors has done as well, where we just cut out the middleman to some extent to supply U.S. patients.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Peter. Camila, portfolio considerations?
Camila Sylvest
EVP of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk A/S
Yeah. We continue to, of course, evaluate how can we optimize our portfolio considerations also for the U.S.. Right now we're very focused on the single-dose device, but of course, over time we are looking at also how can we make efficient dosing of GLP-1s in fixed, you can say, dosing regimens. How can we do that in a smarter way that requires less capacity? It's something that we constantly look at across our value chain. How can we optimize with the presentation formats we have across the world? How can we release more products, and with that, also increase our scalability? Constantly we will be evaluating those things.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Good. Let's go up here to Rajesh.
Rajesh Kumar
Managing Director, Head of Life sciences, and Healthcare Equity Research, HSBC
Hi. Rajesh Kumar for HSBC. One for Martin. It would be unfair of me to ask you to comment on how others would design their clinical trials, but given the data pack we have seen so far on semaglutide, if you were, say, designing next-generation trials for your next-generation products, would you be, say for example, the likes like for a SELECT or CKD, would you be using placebo as a control, or would you be using semaglutide? And what does that mean about, you know, how do you need to power the trial? What size of trial do you need?
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you. Martin, trial design consideration.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo Nordisk A/S
Really complex question and a lot of regulatory considerations also. I think you're actually seeing different approaches across industry right now. We are getting closer to, for example, in obesity, in the cardiovascular space, if there is a gold standard, you can't compare to placebo. You have to compare to that gold standard. That could potentially be semaglutide. That basically means from our perspective, if we, for example, look at CagriSema, if we want to claim the same benefit as semaglutide, we have to show parity with semaglutide or non-inferiority to semaglutide if we did a head-to-head. That would require, I would say, a normalized outcomes trial if going for the same endpoints. If you had to show superiority over semaglutide, obviously we are talking about a taller order.
there we would have to to be looking at obviously the sample size, but also what are the potential endpoints and what are other aspects of the trial design that would allow us to, within reason, demonstrate superiority on the relevant endpoints. You see others adding to the number of composites in the primary endpoint, and that's obviously a vehicle to increase the number of events that you're looking at, and thereby by inference, allowing you to go with a smaller sample size. All of that has to play in. If there's no gold standard, it makes still a lot of sense to compare to placebo. If we look at other aspects of-
Our product's benefits, we would potentially also still be comparing to placebo. CagriSema, for example, is comparing to placebo when it comes to cardiovascular outcomes, and that is basically because at the point in time where we initiated the trial, there was no gold standard.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Martin. Let's go to Richard Vosser here on the front row. We have time for a few more questions.
Richard Vosser
Managing Director, JPMorgan
Hi. Thanks. Richard Vosser from J.P. Morgan. Just a thought on the Part D redesign that we're gonna see next year, how that could impact the net pricing for Ozempic and Rybelsus into 2025. Thanks.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Richard. Karsten, I think this one's for you.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you. First of all, we are in negotiations. This is negotiation season, so formularies haven't played out yet, so it's there's really a lot of uncertainty at this point in time. I would say two pieces to it. There's the redesign, and then there are the negotiations dynamics in Part D. On the redesign, it's important to note that with the redesign benefit design, then yes, there's a benefit because the donut hole is being eliminated, but then there's a different exposure in terms of catastrophic coverage, as well as some other coverage. Net-net, while we initially thought it was directionally positive, now we believe it's broadly neutral on the redesign.
I'd say on the redesign impact to the plan sponsors and hence the insurance companies and how much, how it impacts them, and how much they can pass on to their customers and what that then in turn indirectly impacts us remains to be defined. I would say the competitive situation in the marketplace is unchanged between suppliers into the marketplace. Too early to comment on.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Karsten. Sachin, you had a question, and we'll take Emily afterwards.
Thank you, Sachin.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
For regulatory approval, both improvement in steatosis and fibrosis is required, and the study is designed to look at that. Our dialogue with the FDA was that our phase II trial was never sample sized to look from a statistical perspective on fibrosis. We saw a highly significant reduction in steatosis. We actually saw a great numerical reduction in fibrosis as well. The statement from the FDA was if we saw a similar numerical reduction in a properly sample size study, obviously that would become statistically significant. From a regulatory perspective, that would also be acceptable. Instead of asking us to conduct two phase III studies, they said that the phase II study could serve as one of the two regulatory studies, and we now are doing as the other study.
Sachin Jain
Assistant VP, Bank of America
Is that a 10% delta? If that's repeated in phase III, does that account for that?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Slightly more than 10%. Yes, if that becomes statistically significant, then we are in a good place.
Sachin Jain
Assistant VP, Bank of America
Thank you.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Martin. Thanks. Let's take the last question from Emily, and then we will have time to talk with management afterwards also before they depart.
Emily Field
Director and Lead Analyst European Pharmaceuticals, Barclays
Thank you. Emily Field from Barclays. Going back to Wegovy pricing, I know this was asked yesterday, but there's an FT article today talking about Novo cuts Wegovy price. Maybe to ask a little differently, you know, has the net price evolution for Wegovy in the U.S. been within your expectations? You also mentioned pricing movements in certain channels. I know you'll have more Medicare going forward with Select, but could you just give some granularity on what you meant by that?
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Karsten.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Yeah. Since it's probably me being quoted, I better stand up for it. This is completely as expected. Right. What we're looking at in the market is that this is a volume opportunity, and we're very happy with the market access we have in the U.S.. We have more than 50 million people with obesity covered in the U.S. today. Our market access is very good. Of course, we work with the payers to ensure that we have the appropriate market access that ensures this level of coverage or even more. Of course, the market is also defined through competition and a competitive entry.
There are no surprises in pricing in the U.S.. Just reminding you, this is a significant volume opportunity. The 50 million people with obesity that we have covered for today, we are only serving a fraction of that, less than 1 million.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Karsten. That concludes the Q&A session. Before giving the word to Karsten for his final remarks, I just want to say thanks, Pete, for the kind words, and thanks to all of you that many of you I have met many times over the last four years, and I've truly enjoyed the conversations, the challenging questions, also the pushback. Thank you so much and please remember to keep them on their toes also in the future. Karsten, over to you. Any final words?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Very briefly, thank you for joining again. You feel we're on a roll. Amazing levels of sales growth continuing into this year, 24%, for the quarter, turning into attractive profit growth, 30%, for the quarter at the current exchange rate. Our innovation machine is really also on a roll in terms of readouts and what you just have seen thus far between SELECT, FLOW, and hopefully, to be replicated into the near future, on the coming readouts. Very strong push on innovation for the rest of the year. Thank you for your attention and we'll be around for another quarter or so. Looking forward to discussing more detail. Thank you.
