content.text:
Sachin Jain
Analyst, Bank of America
Operator, we're about to get started. Okay. Should we get everyone seated so we can get kicked off on time? If we can quieten down, we're on quarter past the hour, so we'll try and kick off as we can. Okay, everyone. Should we get kicked off? Thank you very much. Thank you very much, everyone. It's Sachin Jain here from the European pharma team at BofA. Thank you very much to everyone for coming. It's a real pleasure to be hosting Novo post their results. Obviously, we have a fuller room than anticipated. Obviously, Tuesday was a very good day, and so demand built. Apologies we're tight in here. We have an hour and 15. We have the entire C-suite. I think we have half an hour of presentation and questions. Lars, without further ado, over to you. Thank you very much.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Bank of America for hosting us. Indeed it is a great week for us. We're very excited. It's great to be on the road and talk about where the company is. We will go through the slides relatively quickly so we can get into the Q&A. I have to advise you that we'll be making some forward-looking statements, and obviously things can turn out in a different way. Please pay attention to these comments. From an overall strategic aspiration point of view, we feel really good about how we're tracking, both on our purpose and sustainability, but obviously really strong commercial execution.
The 30% growth we had in H1 of this year and the raised guidance underpins both how we are executing commercially, but also how we're confident in building capacity to be able to supply to a higher and higher degree to this amazing growth opportunity. We had a major readout this quarter in R&D, not least this week with the SELECT data, very comforting for the longer term prospects of semaglutide in obesity. It's really a molecule that keeps giving. We have also seen the STEP-HFpEF data really leading data in heart failure space and maybe something that goes a bit below the radar. Had this been, you know, individual trial for a new molecule, I think it would have attracted even more attention.
Really encouraging to see how we're broadening out the potential indications for semaglutide and also the oral data. In the financial quadrant, we'll also explain a bit more about in the slides, really strong growth. We see that we can turn the higher growth momentum into higher operating profits, and here also an increased outlook. Really strong H1 for Novo Nordisk. We're encouraged about our outlook. With that, I'll hand over to Camilla for a few more details on the commercial performance.
Camilla Sylvest
VP of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Lars. When we look at our 30% sales growth, you just see here how it is constituted. I'm just moving in front of the microphone, sorry. A sales growth of 30% driven by both of our operating units. We see North America had 44% growth, IO 17% growth, but also other regions all driving double-digit growth. When we segment the growth into the therapy areas, you see GLP-1 growth of 50%, you see insulin of -7%, and then obesity care of 157%, and Rare Disease of -18%. Basically more than 100% of our growth is driven by diabetes and obesity.
The growth is driven 71% by North America in terms of share growth, and 55% of our sales is now in North America. That of course to a large extent also is constituted of obesity sales growth. I'll just dig into that a little bit more on this slide where you see the 150% sales growth in the H1, mainly driven by the US. You also know that we have done commercial launches in the US, Denmark, and Norway, and most recently in Germany of Wegovy. We have broad commercial access in the US with more than 80% coverage. We are of course continuing to build supply to cater for this market and these patients.
We are also continuing to make sure that we support continuity of care for patients so that those who are starting on the product can keep staying on the product. I'm sure we will talk much more about obesity in the Q&A section also. I hand over now to Martin to talk a little bit more about obesity also.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP of Research and Development and Chief Scientific Officer, Novo Nordisk
Thank you very much, Camilla. I was also asked by Daniel to be brief, and I think when it comes to SELECT, that's reasonably easy. You asked us a lot of questions over the last couple of years about SELECT, and that's been interesting. It's really all about one number, 20%. You've probably seen the data. We are only disclosing the primary endpoint at this point. Obviously to see a 20% risk reduction in MACE in a population as we investigated in SELECT is no less than stellar from our perspective. It's gonna change the way that we see, the way we treat obesity. Obviously with a safety profile that again confirms the safe approach that we have to treatment of obesity with semaglutide, we are really happy with the data that we've seen.
Next steps. I've received a lot of questions already about secondary endpoints, about more details about some of the things that all of us, both from a clinical but also from a payer perspective are interested in. You'll have to wait a couple of months until the American Heart Association will release more data, both at the actual congress but also through publications. Then obviously we are working hard towards a release, sorry, the regulatory submission of this data in Europe and in US to start with. In other R&D news, obviously we are focusing a lot on oral semaglutide in both diabetes and obesity in the sense that we are planning for US submission in Q3 of this year for both diabetes and obesity, 25 mg and 50 mg in diabetes, 50 mg in obesity.
In Europe, in Q4, again for both diabetes and obesity. In CagriSema, we are initiating our phase III program for type 2 diabetes. The reason why you don't see CagriSema in this is basically because phase III has, in terms of recruitment, been finalized for REDEFINE 2 and 3. That basically means that we are in the treatment phase, and we are awaiting results. As a good marker, obviously, we tend to see that it's easier to recruit when patients, physicians are interested in the drug. Even with 5,000 patients almost being recruited in the CagriSema program, we actually finalized recruitment well ahead of time, as compared to our plans. Already talked about SELECT. I think it's important to also call out as a last step the STEP-HFpEF trial where we saw phase III results in obesity.
Really, really strong and interesting data on functionality of semaglutide in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. I think it's also important to call out that these measures of functionality can actually be correlated to outcomes, which is why it's, from a regulatory perspective, also interesting. We can actually expect to see a label update when we combine with the type 2 diabetes results showing the benefits of semaglutide in patients suffering from heart failure. We terminated a PYY agonist program earlier this year, basically based on not sufficient efficacy results, not leading to a differentiated profile. As you know, we have a very strong opinion on not progressing, not differentiated assets.
Maybe in Rare Disease, obviously remind you that somapacitan has been approved in both Europe and Japan for treatment of children with growth hormone deficiency. As some of you also have noticed, we've announced that we've initiated a phase III program for semaglutide. It's actually an outcomes trial in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. With that, over to Karsten.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
CFO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Martin, for a brief and selective presentation. First half results, 30% growth. Of course, looking at the quarters, I would be remiss if not saying 36% growth in the second quarter, probably the strongest growth in the history of the company. For sure it is in absolute terms. Really a staggering growth level delivered through our portfolio as Camilla presented. Through that growth, we're investing in the company, first of all, in our supply chain. We're building our supply chain. We invest in building the obesity market and of course invest in building an attractive and competitive pipeline in both the medium and long term.
Still, we are able to return operating profit growth of 32% and an earnings per share growth for the H1 of 44%. Outlook for the year, we raised both sales and OP outlook by 3% points. That's not even the most impressive part of it, because in reality, our outlook for the year mimics the growth rate we saw in the first half. With 30% in the first half, midpoint for the full year is a 30% growth. Really impressive growth in an industry which is perhaps growing to the tune of low to mid-single digits. Same for operating profit growth, even higher in the sense that we get some gearing, of course, linked to our sales growth.
A guidance now of between 31% and 37% operating profit growth. Currency is unchanged compared to last, and a slight downgrade on our free cash flow. This is purely because our free cash flow definition includes cash flow going to business development activities. As we disclosed, we've done the Biocorp acquisition on connected devices, and we have the Inversago acquisition. Adjusting for that, we're actually increasing our free cash flow in line with the strengthening business outlook. So much for the outlook. Lars on strategic aspirations.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah, I alluded a bit to it in the beginning. We feel real confident, comfortable in how we're progressing on our strategic aspirations. An amazing demand for our GLP-1, GLP-1-based product portfolio. I think we're executing quite well in taking that opportunity and converting that into sales. I think we should also rest assured that we are investing what is needed for us to scale capacities to continuously grow and aim to meet that demand. Pipeline progress is equally important for us. I think we have a very strong underpinned growth opportunity with semaglutide based on the SELECT data. In parallel, we're building late- and early-stage pipeline. We are quite comfortable that we can add that on top of the growth prospect that semaglutide provides.
I'll leave it with that, and we should then go to the Q&A session, which Daniel will moderate. Maybe we should all come up here and stand so we can easily go to the podium.
Moderator
Yes. Thank you, Lars. I'll moderate the Q&A session. Please clearly state your name and institution. Let's go for one question per person, and then we'll take different rounds if time allows. As always, I think we should give the first question to our host, Sachin Jain.
Sachin Jain
Analyst, Bank of America
Gonna be a Sachin Jain from Bank of America. It's gonna be a challenge for me to have one, so I'm gonna have one in two parts, if that's all right. I'm gonna do sema heart failure for a minute. You've mentioned a couple of times you believe it's underappreciated. One to Martin, if you can talk about the correlation of this functional outcomes to hard outcomes and when we see data. ESC in a few weeks, do you get hard outcome data that gets across the 10% to 15% threshold that people, cardiologists typically think clinically relevant? Camilla, very simply, if you could just outline the commercial opportunity as an add-on to standard of care. Thanks.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP of Research and Development and Chief Scientific Officer, Novo Nordisk
Both the KCCQ and the six-minute walk test can be correlated to outcomes. Obviously, it's always a little bit difficult to quantify that correlation. But it is to a level, and it's so well-established that from a regulatory perspective, it's actually possible to get both the six-minute walk test and KCCQ into a label. I think it's important for us to call out that, and again, we can't disclose the data, but we will obviously be looking at also SELECT, where we had at baseline 25% of patients having established heart failure. Therefore we have a big opportunity to look into the SELECT data as a secondary endpoint, and evaluate the semaglutide impact on heart failure.
That will allow us to potentially not only get the functionality assessment into the label, but also, maybe even, hard endpoints, depending of, obviously the data and our interactions with the regulators.
Camilla Sylvest
VP of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Thank you, Martin. In terms of potential, we estimate that approximately 25 million to 30 million people living with HFpEF. Of course, a big, big part of them are living with obesity also. In principle, one could say that the Wegovy label almost cover that, if you say a BMI above 27, and obesity-related comorbidities. It will be very important for us to actually get it in the label so that we're able to promote that. With that, of course, we are able to establish a differentiator with Wegovy compared to other treatments.
Moderator
Thank you, Martin. Thanks, Camilla. We're ready for the next, and I will give to Emily.
Emily Field
Director and Head of US Biopharmaceuticals Equity Research, Barclays
Hi, Emily Field from Barclays. I wanted to follow up on one of Doug Langa's answers yesterday about SELECT maybe having the potential to change the attitude of Medicare. Just how would that work? Is it that you need to have that added to the label first, and then Medicare could have those discussions? And then also, I believe the Treat and Reduce Obesity Act was reintroduced into the Senate, this summer. Any updates on the progression of that legislation?
Moderator
Thanks, Emily. Lars, will you take that?
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. It's a political process, obviously, and it's hard to predict around that. I feel confident that we'll end up having a coverage in Medicare. Exactly when it will happen is hard for us to imagine. You're right that there is now, it seems like there's bipartisan support of that. But I also know there's a lot of other healthcare discussions going on. How this gets priority is hard to say. You can imagine then when a population has been on obesity treatment in, say, the workforce and been active taxpayers and eventually retire, you would also expect to have support for such an intervention there. I think we'll get there.
Short term, it's not something that's rate limiting for our ability to drive growth because we have, you know, maybe 500,000 patients on treatment, and we have access to 45 million patients. There's ample of patients for us to source from short term as we build this broad access. Thank you.
Moderator
We are ready for the next question. We'll give it to Mark Purcell.
Mark Purcell
European Biopharmaceuticals Analyst, Morgan Stanley
Thank you, Daniel. It's Mark Purcell from Morgan Stanley. A question for Martin. Martin, when you look back at outcome trials, including SUSTAIN 6, PIONEER 6, you look at the STEP program, you look at the NASH studies, could you help us understand what percentage of the cardiovascular benefit you believe is weight related, and what percentages is non-weight related? And maybe then to Camilla, how will you educate and promote the message that the quality of weight loss might be different with semaglutide versus competing incretins?
Martin Holst Lange
EVP of Research and Development and Chief Scientific Officer, Novo Nordisk
Thanks very much for what I think is a very important question. Obviously, we can see across the board. Maybe take a step back. When we look at the effect of, for example, semaglutide on cardiovascular benefits, we can look at different variables and their attribution to that effect. We do that through what we call a mediation analysis. In that, we can look at various different parameters. It's relevant, for example, for semaglutide to look at weight loss, to look at glycemic control, to look at blood pressure, to look at lipid lowering, and potentially also to look at inflammation and other factors. We know already from diabetes that it's not just weight loss, it's not just the glycemic control.
In all of our studies, the anti-inflammatory effects of semaglutide has popped up as being quite important, almost up there with weight loss, and the glycemic control. I can't disclose the data from SELECT, but obviously we will do mediation analysis here also to explain what is driving the 20% MACE benefit that we see with semaglutide. My assumption would be that just like we see it in diabetes, it will be in part weight loss, but it will also be the anti-inflammatory effects, but probably also some glycemic control, and the other parameters. I think it's important to take a holistic approach to this. It's not just about the weight loss, it's not just about the glycemic control, but it's the bigger picture of benefits that we see with semaglutide.
Moderator
Thanks, Martin. A quick comment from you, Camilla.
Camilla Sylvest
VP of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Exactly as a follow-up to what Martin is saying, with Wegovy, that is the only product that so far has proven the cardiovascular outcomes reduction in terms of MACE benefits. When we will discuss a little bit more about the elements of that, then that is of course also a clear differentiator for us in terms of how we will promote the product going forward. You will hear much more about that when we publish more details. But what we can promote always depends on what Martin can deliver. That's how things are constructed.
Moderator
Thanks, Camilla. We'll move down here to Pete.
Pete Verdult
Managing Director and Pharmaceuticals Analyst, Citi
Pete Verdult with Citi. One question, Martin, again. REWIND and SUSTAIN, if I recall the event rate with around 9% to 12%. I realize that's a different population, they were diabetics. You know, I'm not asking you to disclose the data of SELECT, but can you just help us? You know, I'm assuming that this population, the assumed event rate was much lower. Is that a fair assumption? Or can you at least tell us going into the study, I don't wanna know the data, but what you were assuming the event rate would be in this population? Thank you.
Moderator
Thanks, Pete. Martin, Pete doesn't want to know the data, but he still had a question.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP of Research and Development and Chief Scientific Officer, Novo Nordisk
You are exactly right. Our assumptions were that typically we see around 4%, maybe a little more, per year. With SELECT, we assumed approximately half of that. I think it's fair to say, without disclosing any data, we were not that far off. Slightly above 2%.
Moderator
Thanks, Martin. We'll move to Simon here.
Simon Baker
Head of Global Biopharma Research, Redburn
Thank you. Simon Baker from Redburn. I'll keep this one a bit more general, because we've been asked this a lot this week, and it's questions on margins and the outlook for margins. That there are two schools of thought that given your growth, there is inevitably significant operational leverage in the business and margins will rise significantly over time. There are others saying that you have a lot of investment in R&D going forward as you broaden your therapeutic base. There are others saying there's only so far you can let margins rise before it becomes an issue with payers. The question is not really such a guidance, but how do we think about that in terms of how far margins could rise and how far margins should rise over time? Thank you.
Moderator
Karsten, I think that's for you.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
CFO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. That's well selected, Simon. So in terms of margin as we commented on before, our starting point being north of 40% in terms of operating margin is top quartile industry. You know, we're not adjusting for anything as you know. So a really competitive starting point. So our strategy as a company in terms of resource allocation is not driven by margin leverage. It's driven by top line growth. Top line growth is really our top priority. Then investing in the business in a rational way. At the last Capital Markets Day, we indicated it would be broadly flat given different puts and takes, especially investing in R&D.
What we didn't fully foresee at the last CMD is quarters like we just passed with 36% growth. As I said at Q1, when we go at this pace, then there will be margin leverage. The magnitude of margin leverage is of course depending on the investment opportunity. If I just go through some of the main puts and takes, then for our gross margin, given the product mix of what's driving top line growth, then that creates a margin gross margin expansion opportunity. Of course, it's partially being offset by some pricing slash geo mix. Secondly, it's also being impacted by our significant CapEx program.
Because part of our CapEx program, even though most goes to the balance sheet, there are certain parts that goes into the P&L. Net-net, slightly improving gross margin, it's already at a high level, as you know, at 85%. SG&A that will have leverage, since we have the infrastructure more or less in place. There will be investments in driving and delivering on the growth opportunities we have. Of course, when we are rate limited on certain products, then of course we don't put more money behind it. That would be value destruction. Then finally in R&D, this really comes back to the opportunities.
We see, when you look at our R&D ratio, then below industry, and of course with the growth rate we have, we also need to replenish our pipeline to build our company for the longer term. That's where we're setting up both in our R&D. When you look at this year in Inversago, you know, I'm not adjusting for anything linked to BD, right? That's part of the 3% point guidance upgrade this year. That covers whatever trial running costs related to Inversago as an example and Biocorp. Expect R&D ratio to go up over time and, net-net, you know, at a this year around 30% sales growth, that will deliver margin expansion. Then we'll come back to more specifically in the years to come, when we comment on top-line guidance, to what extent that opens up for margin expansion.
Moderator
Thanks, Karsten. We're ready for the next.
Jo Walton
Pharma Analyst, Credit Suisse
Jo Walton at Credit Suisse. I'm going to follow on from Simon Baker, I think. Just look at pricing going forward. It's all very well having a drug that you sell to 500,000 people, but if you sell it to 45 million people, society isn't gonna pay anywhere near the same price. I would imagine that at the moment, because everybody, you know, yourselves and Eli Lilly, both in diabetes and obesity are capacity constrained, you're actually okay on pricing. If I look going forward, I wonder how competitive that might be and how low the prices might go. I note, for example, that Kaiser Permanente has removed Ozempic and Trulicity and gone 100% Mounjaro for their Medicare plan, at least that's what it says on the website.
That's giving you an idea that there are payers out there who could just go one way or the other. I was wondering how you felt we should be looking at pricing, 'cause we're very good at assuming that there's massive increase in penetration, and we're not always as good at assuming that the price comes down to match.
Moderator
Thanks, Jo. Karsten or Lars, I don't know who wants to go.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
If you look at our obesity price point, that is somehow historically determined because there was an anchor point in the diabetes indication for Victoza in the market. Because of linearity, we ended up at the price point we are at now. You can say, what is the payer reaction so far? That is actually willingness to pay that. That also goes when the payer is an individual person that has tried, you know, a lot of different attempts to lose weight. I actually think there is an attractive value case, and that value case is just getting better, because many of those patients, as alluded to by Camilla and Martin, are living with a number of diseases.
Now we have a product like Wegovy that's about to unfold in the number of indications that it's actually supporting. Many patients will benefit from all of these indications. We also know that depending on which market we're talking about, that we typically launch at the highest price and then rebates takes it down over time, despite the fact that we actually add more and more value to the product. If you look in the single payer territory like what we have in Europe, I think payers are trying to figure out how can we open up for obesity medicine.
We're also trying to look at how can we actually make sure that when you get to markets, we actually collaborate with single payers in making sure that those who are struggling the most, there is a socio-economic element to obesity also, that those who would not be able to pay out of pocket themselves, that we actually work with healthcare systems to make sure that they are addressed. Acknowledging that no healthcare systems would actually be able to cater for all patients, and then there'll be out-of-pocket segments. I think we'll see different payer channels or structures, so to say, in different markets where we have an opportunity of getting to actually creating a societal impact that's recognized and that the payer will be willing to pay for, whether that's a healthcare system or individuals.
I think we'll have an immense impact on health at a population level by this intervention that I think will be recognized and appreciated. Thank you.
Moderator
We'll go here to Richard.
Richard Parkes
Pharmaceuticals and Biotechnology Equity Analyst, BNP Paribas Exane
Yeah, Richard Parkes from BNP Paribas Exane. Some SELECT, in theory, if you get a secondary prevention label from the FDA, that could allow for Medicare reimbursement. I'm just wondering how confident you are that might be the case and what number of patients or individuals that could unlock. I think it feels like it could be 10 million to 15 million lives in the US. Just wondering if you could talk about that.
Moderator
Karsten, will you take that?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
CFO, Novo Nordisk
Thanks for that question. I think it builds a little bit on what we discussed before. Getting it on label, of course, strengthens our position vis-à-vis that obesity medication should be available for all people with obesity in the US. When we look at the magnitude as Lars covered before, if you look at it today, call it 100 million adults with obesity in the US, almost half of those with insurance coverage and 1% of those with insurance coverage on a known risk medication today, 1%. The runway on what we have currently is fantastic.
With the Medicare coming on, it's a political process, so there's no simple causality between clinical trial outcomes, even though we would like it, and then legislation because it requires a legislative change. That's political process. It will come, we think, but it's politics. Let's see when it comes.
Richard Parkes
Pharmaceuticals and Biotechnology Equity Analyst, BNP Paribas Exane
I suppose my question was.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
CFO, Novo Nordisk
Mm-hmm.
Richard Parkes
Pharmaceuticals and Biotechnology Equity Analyst, BNP Paribas Exane
It could allow for reimbursement via Medicare without legislation.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
CFO, Novo Nordisk
Uh-
Richard Parkes
Pharmaceuticals and Biotechnology Equity Analyst, BNP Paribas Exane
Meaning if it's a secondary prevention.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
CFO, Novo Nordisk
It is a potential, but that's something we're looking into, whether you know whether. It would not be necessarily a slam dunk to get a broader approach to Medicare Part D through the CV benefit or the heart failure trial. That could be some opening vis-a-vis reimbursement, but it's not something that is fully clarified at this point. What would the process be in terms of, you could say, if not the step edits, but the paperwork to get to that reimbursement. That's not clarified at this point. Sorry for not being clear.
Moderator
Thanks, Karsten. We'll move over here.
Rajesh Kumar
Senior Global Healthcare Analyst, HSBC
Hi, Rajesh Kumar from HSBC. Just thank you very much for indicating that, you're putting up R&D, you know, you would invest more. When you think of capital allocation over the next three to five years, which would it be more towards organic R&D or acquisitions? And if so, what are the thresholds you put internally? In that context, if you could help us unpack the latest valuation you paid for the acquisition. You know, what was the thinking behind it? What was the logic and, you know, cannabinoid receptor, you know, a lot of us get worried when we hear about that, but, you know, you found a billion-dollar-plus valuation for that. It would really help if you could unpack that. Thank you.
Moderator
I don't know, Martin, if you will start by giving the rationale from your perspective, and then others can chip in.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP of Research and Development and Chief Scientific Officer, Novo Nordisk
I wanna chip in here. I think when we look at internal versus external innovation, it's very, very clear you will not be successful with external innovation if you don't have very strong internal innovation. Without putting a number, it's very, very clear we have an ambition in all of our disease areas to have strong internal innovation, but then complement our internal innovation with what we can acquire from the external. We also have a very clear approach where we go externally. We're not going for late-stage assets. We're going to look at assets that are in late pre-clinical, early clinical, so we can deliver the value and build on those opportunities. Obviously, there's a little bit of a higher risk, but there's also more value creation by taking this approach.
Specifically for the Inversago, I don't think you should be worried because you're absolutely right with the CB1 antagonism that there have been historically problems. These are molecules that have primarily worked in the central part of the body, so in the brain, where they obviously introduce some efficacy in terms of weight loss, but also some quite serious side effects. With the INV-202, we have a CB1 inverse agonist that primarily works in the peripheral tissue. That actually calls for a really good efficacy, but also calling for minimization of the historical adverse effects because the impact on the brain is minimized. That also means that when we look at the clinical data, it was very clear in the historical trials. It was present in 30% of the patients.
It's pretty easy to spot, and it occurred within two to three weeks after treatment initiation. We can actually allow ourselves to look at the clinical data, even if it's phase I, phase II data that we're looking at, and with some confidence then say that they had actually managed to de-risk this through a peripheral mode of action and not a central mode of action. I think we take a very deliberate approach to how we do external innovation and investment, and I don't think you should be too concerned about the hardware acquisition.
Moderator
Martin, for clarification, Karsten on valuation.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
CFO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Very briefly, the $1 billion you allude to, that's biotech dollars. So we didn't pay $1 billion upfront, just to be clear about that. The way we think about it is basically, you know, we do an asset valuation like we do on our internal projects, including, you know, upfront and whatever subsequent liabilities, and compare that to the risk of the project and the potential future value opportunity in the space. I think this one is, you know, actually, and then we do deal benchmarks on top of that. Pretty straightforward as any other asset acquisition.
On this one specifically, I think it works out nicely between the upfront and the risk and the market opportunity. Then we front load the de-risking of the assets. So from a financial point of view, the CFO is happy.
Moderator
That's good to know, Karsten. David, we'll move to you.
David Evans
Senior Pharma Research Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux
Thanks so much. David Evans from Kepler Cheuvreux. Just a question on the SELECT study population. As I understand, this is kind of a subset of ASCVD patients, basically, so probably less than 10% of the overall obesity population, if that's fair. I mean, can we extrapolate the results to the broader population then, patients who are just at CV risk? I mean, especially given what we saw in LEADER and SUSTAIN 6, that there was, you know, big difference between efficacy in patients with pre-existing CV disease, not really, not much of a trend in patients without. Is it actually a different debate around whether you get coverage in ASCVD patients versus the broader population or will payers look at this somehow as the same population or read across? Thanks.
Moderator
I think, Martin, you can start.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP of Research and Development and Chief Scientific Officer, Novo Nordisk
Maybe also Camilla wants to chip in, we have to distinguish between secondary prevention and primary prevention. What we've done with SELECT is secondary prevention. We've investigated in patients with overweight or obesity and a combination of either primary myocardial infarction or stroke and peripheral artery disease. It's actually a fairly large subpopulation, if you will.
In the obesity space and to Camilla's point, if there's 750 million people out there, even 10% would be a quite sizable. Actually, I think it's slightly above 10%. I don't wanna speculate whether payers will extrapolate to primary prevention. We have seen actually in the diabetes space that there are examples that if you show secondary prevention, you will likely also show primary prevention. We ourselves are looking into primary prevention within diabetes. I think it's fair to say that we will also discuss whether we need to do that within obesity.
At this point in time, I don't think from a commercial perspective it's required, but I think it would be interesting to look at from a clinical perspective, so we can continue to guide our prescribing decisions.
Moderator
Thanks, Martin. Camilla, quick, follow-up.
Camilla Sylvest
VP of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk
Yeah, just very shortly to say that two out of three people living with obesity die from cardiovascular disease, and we know that they incur two to three times higher cost in the healthcare system. Of course with the SELECT data, there's likely to be high interest from payers to understand how we can bring down those costs.
Moderator
Camilla? I'll give the mic to Ben.
Ben Yeoh
Senior Portfolio Manager, RBC Asset Management
Hi, it's Ben Yeoh at RBC Global Asset Management. I had a question, I guess, on human capital and organizational resilience. Would you say your execution is average or above average or maybe even below? You guys are hiring probably at the fastest rate you have ever hired, and that obviously causes a lot of friction. Do you feel that this hiring and the resilience is going well? Do you have enough good people to execute? 'Cause obviously you're a bit supply-constrained now, but you're gonna need, you know, thousands of good people to do this. I'd be interested in some comments on the human capital side. Thanks.
Moderator
I'll give the word to you, Lars.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you. I think it's a great question. We are a people business. It is people at the end of the day that turns the facilities into products, R&D, et cetera. You raise a good point. We have recruited some 8,500 people over a year. If you talk about, say, whether that's working, you say the HR department is working because they have actually recruited these people. The majority of them goes into manufacturing. When you work in manufacturing, obviously you need to work in compliance. There's a significant onboarding task and training task going on. When we talk about ramping up capacity and supply, that's of course a function of that it takes time to train people.
I believe I have to make the disclaimer that I'm biased because I've been with the company for 32 years. I believe we have a unique culture, what we call the Novo Nordisk Way, based on a set of personal values that we actually assess leaders on whether they walk each and every day, and there are consequences of not doing that. I spent quite some time in understanding from newcomers how they assess joining Novo Nordisk. The first comment I typically get is one in relation to the culture and the consistency between what we actually say we do and what we do. Apparently that's a unique feature. I don't know because I've never tried other places than Novo Nordisk.
It's something we really work hard on, and we're right now rolling out say a double down on Novo Nordisk Way onboarding as an education, 'cause among those 8,500 new colleagues are also leaders. It's really, really important for me and my colleagues and each and everyone walk the talk in terms of culture. I think that's the best guarantee for turning that investment in people into to assets that helps patients at the end of the day.
Moderator
Thanks, Lars. Oh, we have one here.
Harry Gillis
Healthcare Equity Research Analyst, Berenberg
Thank you. Harry Gillis from Berenberg. So just a quick question on oral Wegovy, and whether you can give any indication when you may look to, assuming approval, when you may launch this product. I'm just trying to understand a sense of how viable a large scale launch would be given the sort of higher API requirements, and sort of do you feel confident that maybe in the sort of medium term you'll be able to meet those requirements? If I may also ask just, I know you may not sort of give any details, but at a high level, how you may think about pricing the sort of oral version versus the injectable. Thank you.
Moderator
Thanks for that question. Camilla?
Camilla Sylvest
VP of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk
While I cannot comment on pricing at this point in time, I can comment on the perspectives of 50 mg semaglutide. Of course, we are very happy with the results that shows similar efficacy to Wegovy 2.4 mg. When we are looking at time to launch, we first need this approved. After approval, we will be considering how we can scale this depending, of course, on demand and capacity. I'm saying that because of course you all know that an oral version requires more API than an injectable version.
This rollout of course is likely to be depending on how things are developing at that point in time in terms of demand and supply, knowing that we want to make sure we can cater for as many patients as possible. The demand right now seems to be, of course, very high. Therefore, those are the considerations we have, but much more about that when it's all approved.
Moderator
Thank you so much, Camilla. We have time for a few more questions. I think we're back at our host.
Sachin Jain
Analyst, Bank of America
Thank you very much. It's Sachin Jain from Bank of America again. I'll one for Martin and then one big picture. We didn't really discuss triple-G much at ADA, and you had a similar mechanism internally that you sort of preferred CagriSema. Just any perspectives on how you believe your follow-on compares to Lilly's follow-on? I guess if you could just comment on your perspective on safety. Then their diabetes profile, because I don't think they've started a phase III in diabetes. Then the big picture for Lars, this is a question I get a fair bit, and I'm not sure it's a straightforward answer. GLP-1 consensus at peak across Novo and Lilly is in the $80 billion to $100 billion range now.
The question I frequently get even post-SELECT is how can the system digest a number much bigger than that? I wonder if you can touch on that from a couple of aspects in terms of indication breadth, how you think about cash pay of the market. You know, will the payers digest a much bigger percentage of the pie being a single molecule drug class? Thanks.
Moderator
Thanks, Sachin. We'll start with you, Martin, followed by Lars.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP of Research and Development and Chief Scientific Officer, Novo Nordisk
I'll not do a direct comparison between our pipeline and our competitors, but I think I can do maybe an indirect in the sense that we also had a triple-G in our pipeline a couple of years ago. We obviously also did a clinical assessment of that. In that we obviously found it works, it gives a good weight loss, and it could potentially also have a good impact in NASH. It was more difficult in the diabetes space. There is some inherent challenges in that with glucagon and maybe the combination and the ratios can rectify that a little bit. We also saw other safety issues in the cardiovascular space and had some concerns about the protein metabolism effects of glucagon as well.
Given that we had CagriSema and we had a triple-G in our pipeline, and we actually saw better efficacy with CagriSema and a more clean safety profile from a pipeline perspective, that was an easy choice. Therefore, I don't wanna speculate what others are doing. I wish them best of luck. I think from an efficacy perspective, we'll see it works. Obviously again, we are very confident with the efficacy of CagriSema, both in diabetes and in obesity, and we're also very confident of the safety profile of CagriSema in diabetes and obesity.
Moderator
Thanks, Martin. Lars?
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. I think there's no doubt that the GLP-1 opportunity is a very sizable one, and your guess about how large this can become is as good as ours. I think it's important to dissect this into a number of health benefits. We started looking at type 2 diabetes. We added CV benefit to that. We're now looking at obesity, adding CV benefit to that. We spoke about the HFpEF data in the SELECT study. We studied a number of other outcomes.
I think to really assess how big is this drug class and what does it mean for payers, we actually need to start segmenting the value story from a medical benefit position and the population we serve living with, let's say broad cardiometabolic disorders; they would otherwise end up on say, a handful or two handful of different individual medicines to deal with these medical conditions. I think it's really, really attractive if there's one mechanism that can do it all. I think it creates flexibility in actually how you can define the value story for payers because they can attribute different values depending on which population they look at. I think that's a really, really attractive case for us to be engaged in. Thank you.
Moderator
One final question before we wrap up, but there'll still be time for networking.
Mark Purcell
European Biopharmaceuticals Analyst, Morgan Stanley
That's kind. Thank you. Mark Purcell from Morgan Stanley. Martin, could you give us your latest thoughts on oral approaches for obesity? Small molecules versus peptides, I guess covered in this, in SemaDapa. The decision not to move forward though, was that a technical reason why you're not moving forward? Can you combine small molecules with the SNAC technology, or is there something that you can't do there? It's the question of now having done the Inversago deal, and you've talked about combinations. Are you looking at small molecules plus small molecule combinations or can you combine peptides and small molecules together?
Moderator
Thanks, Mark. Martin?
Martin Holst Lange
EVP of Research and Development and Chief Scientific Officer, Novo Nordisk
I think both in the incretin space, but also moving across the incretin space, it's always relevant to look at different modalities. That obviously comes also to small molecule versus peptide based. From our perspective, what we've seen with the OASIS program, with the PIONEER PLUS program, I think if we just look at GLP-1, it's gonna be from an efficacy and safety perspective difficult to show even better efficacy or safety as compared to that. Obviously that's why we are excited with the PIONEER PLUS and the OASIS data. I think broadly speaking if we move then beyond, for example, to Inversago combination is interesting. I think we see that with our own CagriSema.
We see that also from some of our competitors in order to increase efficacy, but without having to compromise on safety. We can do that in loose combination, combining a subcutaneous and an oral, but we could potentially also be looking at combining potential small molecules with small molecules. Specifically on SemaDapa, you are absolutely right. We terminated that on technical reasons, basically because it was not really a differentiated profile we saw. Showing superiority to the monocomponents is requiring a really big development program that was maybe not really warranted in this space.
Moderator
Thank you, Martin. That concludes our Q&A session. We'll still have a bit of time for networking and opportunity to talk with management. Before we close finally, Lars, any final words from you?
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Just like to take this opportunity to thank Sachin and Bank of America for hosting us, for all of you coming, and the good questions and also you participating on the live stream. As you can hopefully hear, we're hugely excited about the momentum in Novo Nordisk right now. We're equally excited about both the short and the medium long-term growth prospects of the portfolio of products we have and what we have in our pipeline. We look forward to report back to you in the coming quarters on this progress. Thank you.

content.text:
Operator
Good day and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Q4 2022 Novo Nordisk A/S Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press star one one on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message advising your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today, Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen, CEO. Please go ahead.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, operator. Welcome to this Novo Nordisk earnings call for the full year of 2022 and the outlook for 2023. My name is Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen, and I'm the CEO of Novo Nordisk. With me today, I have Executive Vice President and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Camilla Sylvest, Executive Vice President and Head of North America Operations, Doug Langa, Executive Vice President and Head of Development, Martin Holst Lange, and finally, Chief Financial Officer, Karsten Munk Knudsen. All of us will be available for the Q&A session. Today's announcement and the slides for this call are available on our website, novonordisk.com. Please note that the call is being webcasted live, and a recording will be made available on our website as well. This call is scheduled to last one hour. Please turn to the next slide.
The presentation is structured as outlined on slide two. Please note that all sales and operating profit growth statements will be at constant exchange rates unless otherwise specified. Please turn to slide three. As always, I need to advise you that this call will contain forward-looking statements. These are subject to risk and uncertainty that could cause actual results to differ materially from expectations. For further information on the risk factors, please see the company announcement for the full year of 2022 and the slides prepared for this presentation. Please turn to the next slide. In 2022, we delivered double-digit sales growth and operating profit growth, and we continued to make progress on our strategic aspirations. I would like to go through the highlights before handing over the word to my colleagues. We continue to make progress across all dimensions of purpose and sustainability.
Our carbon emissions decreased by 29% compared to pre-pandemic levels in 2019, and we continue to reach even more patients living with diabetes compared to last year. In line with our aspiration of being a sustainable employer, we expanded the number of women in leadership positions to 39% compared to 36% in 2021. Within R&D, we are pleased that we now have initiated the first two phase I trials based on the Dicerna interference RNA technology platform that we acquired in 2021. Looking back at 2022, we have seen exciting trial readouts across all our therapy areas, and in 2023, we look forward to having an equally exciting year. Martin will come back to this and our overall R&D milestones later. In 2022, we delivered double-digit sales growth, reflecting strong commercial execution across geographies and our therapy areas.
While both operating units contributed to sales growth, we saw particularly strong sales growth in North America, driven by accelerated demand for our GLP-1 treatments for both diabetes and obesity. Camilla and Doug will go through the details per therapy area later. Karsten will go through the financials, but I'm very pleased with the sales growth of 16% and operating profit growth of 15% in 2022. Lastly, I have a brief update on our strategic aspirations within financials. We have achieved the US aspiration of converting 70% of sales to products launched since 2015, and IO sales growth has in the last couple of years surpassed aspiration of 6% to 10% growth. Consequently, we have decided to remove these regional aspirations. Going forward, we'll be focused on and committed to delivering solid sales and operating profit growth.
With that, I'll give the word to Camilla for an update on execution.
Camilla Sylvest
EVP and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Lars, and please turn to the next slide. As Lars mentioned, our 16% sales growth for the full year of 2022 was driven by both operating units, with North America operations growing by 21% and international operations growing 13%. The strong sales growth has unfortunately resulted in periodic supply constraints and related stock shortages notifications across a number of products and geographies. Our GLP-1 sales increased by 42%, driven by North America growing 36% and international operations growing 57%. Insulin sales decreased by 11%, driven by a 7% decline in international operations and a 21% sales decline in North America operations. The US insulin sales declined by 22%. This was driven by lower realized prices as well as a decline in volume.
Compared to 2021, the US insulin volume market declined by 3%. Furthermore, insulin sales in International Operations were impacted by the implementation of volume-based procurement in China starting in May 2022, and lower sales in EMEA. Obesity Care sales grew by 84% overall. In International Operations, sales grew by 82%, and in North America Operations, Obesity Care sales grew 85%. In the US, Obesity Care sales grew by 90%. Rare disease sales grew 1%, driven by a 5% sales increase in International Operations, offset by a 5% decline in North America Operations. Please turn to slide six. When it comes to how much of the Wegovy sourcing that is from diabetes, then we can say that the uplift in the Wegovy trends in the US is basically from primarily the 0.25 starter dose. That basically means that these are patients that are new to GLP-1 treatment. Of course, looking forward, that means that we expect that there is a potential for both of these two classes to coexist and to continue increasing as we see both unexplored potential for GLP-1 treatment in diabetes as well as in obesity.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Camilla, Doug, on the payer's perspective, multiple years of treatment.
Doug Langa
EVP and Head of North America Operations, Novo Nordisk
Yeah, Richard, thank you. I think it's important to note that we're pleased with the level of access that we have today. Overall, 80% access is something that we're proud of, and the team has done a nice job. Effective access, we've been hard at work at. As you know, this requires opt-ins. But again, we're pleased with the overall 40 million lives that can have access. How the payers are treating this, there's no stopping rules in place today. I think the payers recognize that this is a chronic treatment, and that's important for not only stakeholders, payers, but all the work that we're doing is to realize this as a serious chronic disease, and it's a chronic disease that needs long-term treatment.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Camilla. Thank you, Doug. Thank you, Richard. Next question, please.
Operator
Thank you. We will now take the next question. It comes from the line of Michael Leuchten from UBS. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
Michael Leuchten
Managing Director of Equity Research, UBS
Thank you. Two questions, please. Michael Leuchten from UBS. One, if I look at the value of the volume for Ozempic and Rybelsus in the US, there seem to be some trend changes in Q4, maybe Ozempic also in Q3. Is that a fair reflection of the competitive rebating environment, or should we not overinterpret those trends as we think about the value to volume looking into 2023? And then a question for Martin. SELECT isn't really something you talk about actively anymore. It only really comes up in Q&A.
Is that because in your mind the relevance has taken a step back given it didn't stop at the interim and we're maybe on track for the 17% risk reduction which may or may not be as meaningful as maybe a 25% would have been? Or is there another reason why you don't mention it as much anymore as you have in the past? Thank you.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Michael. First, Karsten on value versus volume dynamics for GLP-1 products.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
CFO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah, Michael, first of all, to your Q4 questions versus 2022 or then there are no changes vis-a-vis 2022. As you know, normally for 2024 then we give the GLP-1 scripts, then there will be true ups, normally in Q4 that can impact the volume-to-volume equation. I think the more appropriate way to look at it is for the full year. I would say on top of that, given the supply situation on Ozempic, there might be also some noise in that calculation from changes in inventory levels on Ozempic, specifically.
From there moving into 2023, while not guiding for volume for 2023, I would say the dynamics remain the same between 2022 and 2023.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Karsten. Martin, on SELECT, why are you not talking about SELECT?
Martin Holst Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
First of all, we are still very excited and very confident about SELECT. Issue is obviously that we have no results to share, we have no data to share. Therefore, the only thing I can call out, which hopefully you also saw in my part of the presentation, is that we are looking very much forward to the data coming out around mid-2023, and that will be incredibly exciting. We still think SELECT is very important and very exciting.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you. That's very clear. Thank you, Michael. Next question, please.
Operator
Thank you. We will now take the next question. It comes from the line of Keyur Parekh from Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead, your line is open.
Keyur Parekh
Managing Director, Goldman Sachs
Hi. Thank you. Hopefully you can hear me okay. Two separate lines of questioning, please. The first one on CapEx. At the 2022 Capital Markets Day, your slides implied CapEx for 2025 to be between kind of DKK 10 and 15 billion. What you're guiding to today implies CapEx close to DKK 25 to 30 billion in 2025. Just wondering if you can give us a sense for kind of how much of that doubling of CapEx is attributable to your perception of higher demand for the existing products. So Wegovy, kind of Rybelsus or GLP-1 diabetes products versus how much of this is with a view to ensuring supply for the non-diabetes, non-obesity product as that pipeline emerges over the course of the next kind of two to three years. That's kind of question number one.
Separately, kind of coming back to icodec. Camilla, I'd love your thoughts on how you think ONWARDS 1 and ONWARDS 6, the extension data, changes, if at all, the commercial positioning kind of for this molecule from your perspective. Does this make it a bit more of an international product compared to a US product given the convenience at play here? Or do you still think there exists room for you to have differential pricing for this molecule in the US given the extension data? Thank you.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Keyur. Two very clear questions. First, Karsten, on CapEx versus what we said at Capital Markets Day and a perspective on, you know, existing products, new areas. Camilla, you can talk to the icodec, say, commercial opportunity.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
CFO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Thank you, Lars. CapEx, of course, quite a significant step up compared to our capital markets day. Again, that's why we're forward-looking statements. The world has a tendency to change these days, more than usual. I would say this step up in CapEx, to me, comes on a very positive background. I can unfortunately not kind of separate how much is what because we have both phasing and the different shared platforms. It is a little bit trying to separate hot and cold water, unfortunately, Keyur. I would say the main drivers to it is first of all, stronger volume uptake than what we had built into our initial CapEx modeling, clearly.
The stronger volume uptake impacts both on the API side of our current marketed products, as well as the fill-finish that we're scaling more so than initially planned. Then as to the pipeline, I would say there are two main drivers to step up. You could say in a historic perspective where we were like call it between 5% and 10% CapEx to sales, and now we're more in call it between 10% and 15% CapEx to sales ratio towards 25%. The delta is that historically it was injectable peptide-based CapEx investments we're doing, and we continue to do that through the volume scaling I just spoke about.
On top of that, we are building to cater for the oral platform that just requires significantly higher amounts of API, whether it's for Rybelsus, oral semaglutide obesity or some of the earlier oral compounds. As you know, we have oral incretin in phase I, and we have an oral GLP-1/GIP also. Clearly for the oral platform and then for the non-protein peptide platforms, I would say we're looking at what we are doing to cater for pipeline assets like amycretin and ziltivekimab and our NN6535 as well, which is on an antibody platform. That's where we're looking at also expanding our capacity on the monoclonal antibody side.
I hope that provides a little bit of color, but not fully able to separate the hot and the cold water.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Karsten. Exciting pipeline leads to need for CapEx. Camilla, how excited are you on icodec, based on the recent data?
Camilla Sylvest
EVP and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Thank you, Lars. As we just discussed before, we remain very confident in the efficacy and safety profile of icodec. That, given as a once-weekly insulin, has the potential to become standard of care for people with type 2 diabetes. To your question, this has not changed our perspectives in terms of a global rollout of icodec. We remain equally confident in the US and in the rest of the world for how this can help people with type 2 diabetes. Keep in mind that the potential of this is that the basal segment approximately includes 30 million patients with a value of around $8 billion. That's a place where we today have a market share in the ballpark of one-third.
There's ample potential to increase that.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Thank you, Camilla. Thank you, Keyur. Next, question, please.
Operator
Thank you. We will now take the next question. It comes from the line of Simon Baker from Redburn. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
Simon Baker
Partner and Head of Global Biopharma Research, Redburn
Thank you for taking my questions. Two, if I may, please. Firstly, this relates to some earlier questions. In recent years, the increased spend in the US on GLP-1 was offset by lower spending on insulin, which gave some easy headroom for the category to expand. I just wonder if you could give us an update on whether that is still the case. Secondly, with Karsten, you talked about the impact of the Dicerna acquisition on Q4 R&D. I just wondered if you'd give us an idea how much of the additional R&D expense incurred was one-off and how much is continuing. Thanks so much.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Simon. I don't know if you have those data, Doug, from the top of your head.
Doug Langa
EVP and Head of North America Operations, Novo Nordisk
What I would say is this, that insulin, as you saw, as we just reported, continues to be under pressure, pricing pressure. Payers still continue to take value there. As I mentioned earlier, there's still only approximately 10% of the prescription volumes coming out of GLP-1. We still think that there's opportunity there.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
You can add that the DPP-4 price decline and soon to come SGLT2 will also create some space to fund innovation. Karsten, on Dicerna, R&D one-off versus continued impact.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
CFO, Novo Nordisk
Simon, as we've been communicating all along, in terms of our overall strategic resource allocation, then we are highly focused on allocating additional resources towards R&D to expand and diversify our pipeline. That you're seeing throughout the year with a significant step up in R&D spend, you know, ending at 29% for the full year. You're right that in Q4 we have an extraordinary step-up also when you do the quarterly trending. It's basically due to two factors.
One, one being a minor impairment on intangible assets, and another piece being costs related to the Forma Therapeutics transaction and restructuring. As you recall, then here at Novo, we are reporting clean numbers. Where other companies would have been, some other companies have been adjusting this into core earnings or adjusted earnings, then here you get what you see is what you get. As to a specific number for Q4, in round terms, between the two impairments and the former, around half a billion DKK.
Simon Baker
Partner and Head of Global Biopharma Research, Redburn
Perfect. Thank you very much.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Simon. We have time for the final question.
Operator
Thank you. We will now take the next question. It comes from the line of Mattias Häggblom from Handelsbanken. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
Mattias Häggblom
Equity Research Analyst, Handelsbanken
Thank you so much. Two questions, please. Firstly, with regards to the decision in January to double down and initiate the high-dose semaglutide obesity trial, I'm curious to understand what triggered the decision and why now, almost one and a half years after the degludec approval, and why not earlier? Secondly, with top line data from SELECT due mid-2023, what's a reasonable timeframe from top line results and the data can help facilitate reimbursement outside the US, a year, or is it rather two, given the size and complexity of the study?
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Okay. Thank you, Mattias. To you, Martin, high-dose semaglutide obesity, why now?
Martin Holst Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Yep. First of all, we see emerging data suggesting that it is possible to max out on GLP-1 biology. And it's very, very clear based on some of our recent studies that we could potentially increase exposure and thereby accruing more weight loss than what we see with the current doses. This obviously we have to pursue, we have to investigate because there is an opportunity to without compromising on safety to accrue even more weight loss, specifically in obesity, and potentially also improve glycemic control in diabetes.
We aim to conduct these studies very fast, and that also means that they will be available to patients if the data supports it, in a not too distant future and still well within the relevant time period for semaglutide.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
There was a question on timeline from SELECT data to reimbursement. Ballpark without going into too much detail.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Some of you have heard about us bragging about being able to obviously handle our clinical data in a reasonable way. I would not be looking at a one to two-year timeline. Obviously, we will close down the study. We will have the results around mid this year. We'll do a regulatory file, and then we'll have the regulatory interactions. Then it's in the US up to Doug and his team to discuss with payers and others on how that will impact the dynamics.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Martin. Thank you, Mattias, and thank you all for participating in our earnings call. Please reach out to our investor relations officer if you have more questions and look forward to meet you and talk to you in the near future. Thank you very much. Bye-bye.
Operator
That does conclude our conference for today. Thank you for participating. You may all disconnect.
